title: Needles in the Haystack: Addressing Signal Dilution Improves scRNA-seq Perturbation Response Modeling and Evaluation
claim: Unweighted error metrics let uninformative mean predictions look good because sparse signal is diluted; weighted, baseline-calibrated metrics and objectives fix this.
layout: 3 stacked panels A-C, each left-to-right, heatmap strips and toy plots
description: A three-row figure with rounded pale-blue panels. Panel A, 'Control Bias', shows a cloud of blue dots with a green control point and a chain of increasingly dark green points. Arrows labeled Δ^all and Δ^p run toward the mean points, and a scatter on the right shows correlation r(Δ^p, Δ^all) rising as control bias increases. Panel B, 'Signal Dilution/Mode Collapse', shows red/blue gene-expression strips for μ^all and μ^p, with the biological-signal genes boxed. Next to them are grayscale error strips for regular MSE weights and DEG-based weights. A small neural network sends two arrows, MSE Loss and Weighted MSE Loss, to dot clouds, one collapsed and one spread out. Panel C, 'Metric Scale Calibration/WMSE Performance', shows a cell-by-gene heatmap, random sampling into predicted and ground-truth halves, and a bar chart of R²_w(Δ) for control, mean, MSE model, WMSE model and technical duplicate.
caption: (A) Under increasing amounts of systematic control bias, the Pearson correlation between ∆p and ∆all increases artificially. (B) True biological signal is diluted in scRNA-seq data causing mode collapse in model predictions. Introducing biologically aware weights (WMSE) ameliorates this problem. (C) We introduce metrics with a performance scale calibrated by negative and positive baselines. We also find that WMSE as a training objective improves model performance compared to MSE.
abstract: Recent benchmarks reveal that single-cell perturbation response models are often outperformed by simply predicting the dataset mean. Through large-scale *in silico* simulations, together with analyses of two real-world perturbation datasets, we trace this anomaly to a metric artifact: unweighted error metrics systematically reward mean predictions when perturbation effects are sparse. To address this limitation, we introduce differentially expressed gene (DEG)-aware metrics—weighted mean-squared error (WMSE) and weighted delta $R^{2}$ ($R^{2}_{w}(\Delta)$)—that sensitively measure error in niche, perturbation-specific signals. We further propose explicit negative and positive performance baselines to calibrate these metrics. Under this framework, the mean baseline sinks to null performance, while genuinely informative predictors are correctly rewarded. Finally, we show that using WMSE as a training objective reduces mode collapse and improves predictive performance across multiple model architectures.
